newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada opens heart to famed Vietnam napalm victim.
newsitem.headline: Canada opens heart to famed Vietnam napalm victim.

text.p: Canadians have opened their hearts and wallets to Phan Thi Kim Phuc, the terrified girl immortalized in a famous photograph of a napalm attack in Vietnam, who is battling poverty in her adopted Canada.

Hundreds of supportive letters and more than C$30,000 ($21,900) in cash have poured in for Kim Phuc since the Toronto Star, Canada's largest newspaper, printed a story six weeks ago about her fight to build a life in Canada.

Kim Phuc, now 33 and pregnant with her second child, lives with her husband Bui Huy Toan and their 4-year-old son in a cramped one-bedroom apartment in Toronto. Her husband works two part-time jobs, while Kim Phuc cares for her son at home.

The Pulitzer prize-winning photo of nine-year-old Kim Phuc fleeing burning and naked -- arms outstretched in pain and terror -- from her napalmed village, galvanized anti-war sentiment in the United States and changed her life.
She is still wracked with pain from her injuries from the 1972 attack and she refuses to wear short sleeves, which would expose some of the burns that scar most of her body.
Kim Phuc told Reuters on Wednesday she did not know what she would do with the money that was donated, but that she was deeply touched by the cash and letters.
"It's wonderful, wonderful. It will help me a lot," she said. "All I can say is, 'Thank you.'"

Kim Phuc and her family were hiding in a South Vietnamese temple when napalm bombs were dropped on her village. The jellied gasoline vaporized her clothes, left her with third-degree burns over half her body and killed two of her younger brothers.

Rescued by Associated Press photographer Nick Ut, who took the award winning photo, Kim Phuc had 17 operations and was used after the war by the communist North Vietnamese for anti-American propaganda.

As a young adult, Kim Phuc was sent to study in Cuba, where she met and fell in love with fellow Vietnamese student Toan. After honeymooning in Moscow in 1992, the couple defected to Canada on a refueling stop en route back to Cuba.

Kim Phuc and her husband were on welfare in Toronto for three years as they struggled to learn English. The family lives on the meager income from Toan's job caring for mentally disabled adults at two group homes.
They have become born-again Christians and said their faith helped them trust in a better future.
Kim Phuc, who has been the subject of several documentaries and retrospectives on the horrors of war, remains a symbolic political presence.
Last November she was the centerpiece of an emotional Veterans Day service in Washington, where she brought her message of peace and forgiveness to Vietnam veterans.

"Even if I could talk face to face with the pilot who dropped the bombs I would tell him, 'We cannot change history, but we should try to do good things for the present and for the future to promote peace,'" she said.
Kim Phuc's greatest wish is to see her family again. So far she has been blocked by political and financial obstacles from visiting her parents and five surviving siblings in Vietnam.
